enrichment.short_title: Prosecution appeal allowed where magistrates wrongly treated expert hypothetises as rebutting s15(3) breath-alcohol presumption
key_facts: Lisa Chambers was charged with driving with excess alcohol after a breath reading of 124 micrograms; she admitted consuming alcohol before and after driving.
Forensic experts agreed only on two post-driving consumption scenarios and not on her interview admission of pre-incident vodka.
Magistrates accepted a submission of no case to answer, treating the joint expert statement as rebutting the section 15(2) presumption.
Prosecution appealed by case stated; the parties agreed to proceed on the shorter interview record showing pre-incident vodka consumption.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by case stated from Sutton Coldfield Magistrates' Court to the High Court (Administration).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; magistrates' decision quashed and matter remitted for rehearing before a differently constituted bench; respondent ordered to pay £500 towards prosecution costs.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 15(3) Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 submission of no case to answer, magistrates must consider all relevant evidence including the defendant's admissions, may not treat unproved expert hypothetises as evidence rebutting the presumption, and act irrationally if expert evidence on the TF7 scenario could not on any view discharge the defendant's burden on the balance of probabilities.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates erred in acceding to no case to answer on excess alcohol where only expert hypothetises were considered
Proper application of section 15(2)-(3) presumption and rebuttal where alcohol was consumed after driving
Whether remittal should be for continuation or rehearing before a fresh bench

enrichment.short_title: Conviction appeal dismissed on hearsay and summing-up grounds; total sentence reduced from seven to four and a half years
key_facts: Bright was convicted at Cambridge Crown Court on eleven counts of indecent assault and indecency with a child against five complainants between 1967 and 1982.
Counts relating to Lynne Herbert were left on the file; defence sought to adduce passages from her unused statement to attack collusion.
The trial judge refused to permit selective hearsay from Lynne Herbert's statement as insufficiently relevant collateral matter.
Total consecutive sentences of seven years' imprisonment were imposed after an earlier Cardiff conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction with leave and against sentence following partial leave/refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; appeal against sentence allowed in part with total sentence reduced to four and a half years' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a non-witness's statement is not before the jury and the Crown does not rely on it, cherry-picked hearsay from that statement is not admissible simply to invite an inference of untruthfulness by live witnesses; the trial judge's discretion to exclude such collateral credit evidence will not be interfered with unless plainly wrong, and long-delayed historical sexual offences may still attract substantial but not excessive consecutive sentences.
legal_issues: Admissibility of selective passages from an unused witness statement under Subramanian v Public Prosecutor
Need for alibi direction where complainant's dates overlapped appellant's Aden service
Fairness of character direction where previous convictions were adduced by the defendant
Whether specimen counts and delay directions rendered verdicts unsafe
Totality and length of sentence given delay and prior Cardiff sentence

enrichment.short_title: Sub-agents without direct principal contract excluded from Commercial Agents Regulations; fixed-term expiry is termination
key_facts: Nine self-employed sales agents sold Ty Europe cuddly toys through Swallow Corporate Sales Ltd after a 1997 restructuring.
Agents had contracts with SCS, not Ty Europe, though retailers and Ty Europe dealt with them as Ty's representatives.
When a three-year selling-rights agreement expired in 2000 the agents declined employment and claimed Regulation 17 compensation from Ty Europe.
Judge McGonigal answered preliminary issues in the agents' favour; Ty Europe appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) from preliminary issue determinations in the Leeds Mercantile Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the sub-agency question (no direct agency contract with principal); effluxion-of-time point answered correctly at first instance but not required for disposal; action dismissed; interim payment of £60,000 to be repaid; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 2(1) defines who is a commercial agent by factual continuing authority, but the substantive protections in the Regulations—including Regulation 17 compensation—require a direct agency contract between agent and principal; sub-agents contractually bound only to an intermediary are not covered, though 'termination' in Regulation 17 includes expiry of a fixed term by effluxion of time.
legal_issues: Whether sub-agents with authority delegated via an intermediary may claim compensation directly against the manufacturer/principal
Whether automatic expiry of a fixed-term agency contract constitutes 'termination' for Regulation 17 purposes
Whether compensation is payable in principle where a single fixed-term contract ends without renewal

enrichment.short_title: Partial leave to appeal granted on Creebeck surplus land and pre-notice interest under 1995 local government property regulations

statutes_considered.title: Local Government Changes for England (Property Transfer and Transitional Payments) Regulations 1995

key_facts: Arbitration awards between Durham County Council and Darlington Borough Council arose from Darlington's creation as a unitary authority on 1 April 1997.
Disputes concerned classification of airport and waste company shareholdings and whether Creebeck waste disposal land was surplus.
A second award addressed whether interest was payable before service of a regulation 16 notice and whether section 49(3) could fill any lacuna.
Durham sought leave to appeal several points of law under section 69.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave to appeal points of law arising from two statutory arbitrations under regulation 19 of the 1995 Regulations, heard by Blackburne J.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted on the Creebeck surplus-land question and on both interest questions; leave refused on airport shareholding and regulation 5(6) issues; permission to appeal Blackburne J's decision to the Court of Appeal refused; costs to be assessed on successful issues.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 69(3) Arbitration Act 1996, questions of general public importance arising from enduring 1995 local government property-transfer regulations may attract leave where the tribunal's decision is at least open to serious doubt; here the Creebeck surplus-land construction and the arbitrator's treatment of pre-regulation-16 interest under regulations 17-18 and section 49(3) met that threshold, whereas the airport share and regulation 5(6) holdings did not.

Whether shares and Creebeck land were held/required for Darlington functions under regulation 5(6) or were surplus land under regulation 10(7)
Whether a paying authority must pay interest before a regulation 16 notice
Whether section 49(3) Arbitration Act 1996 can award interest where the statutory scheme is silent

enrichment.short_title: Takeover scheme of arrangement sanctioned despite shareholder's Article 1 Protocol objection to compulsory cash buy-out
key_facts: Waste Recycling Group plc sought court sanction of a recommended takeover by Cholet Acquisitions Ltd at 267.5p cash per share.
The scheme cancelled all shares and reissued them to the acquirer funded by a capital reduction and share premium account.
Approximately 99.7% by value of votes cast supported the scheme, including a 45.5% principal shareholder.
Minority shareholder Mr Page objected that environmental stewardship interests in public ownership engaged Article 1 Protocol 1 differently from purely financial interests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Petition to the Companies Court to sanction a scheme of arrangement under section 425 and confirm the associated capital reduction.
enrichment.outcome: Scheme sanctioned and capital reduction confirmed; shareholder's Article 1 Protocol 1 objection rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Section 425 scheme approval binding dissentient shareholders is consistent with Article 1 Protocol 1 where shareholders receive consideration and are treated equally; the court looks to shareholders' legal rights under the scheme, not to subjective non-financial motivations for holding shares, and cannot create differential classes based on how shareholders value their interests.
legal_issues: Whether statutory majorities fairly represented the single class of members
Whether capital reduction requirements were satisfied
Whether compulsory cancellation of shares for cash breached Article 1 Protocol 1 where a shareholder claimed environmental/public-interest reasons for retaining shares

enrichment.short_title: Towed engineering plant counted as trailer for tachograph weight limit; Nissan Cabstar appeal dismissed

statutes_considered.title: Community Drivers' Hours and Recording Equipment (Exemptions and Supplementary Provisions) Regulations 1986
Goods Vehicles (Ascertainment of Maximum Gross Weights) Regulations 1976

key_facts: Colin Pritchard drove a 3,400 kg plated Nissan Cabstar towing a single-axle Bocker H16 hoist for Industrade partnership business.
No tachograph was fitted; train weight exceeded applicable limits once the hoist was treated as a trailer.
Partners Stefan Devenish and Pritchard were convicted under section 97 Transport Act 1968 and absolutely discharged.
The hoist was engineering plant not primarily constructed to carry a load but designed to be coupled to a motor vehicle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Leigh/Wigan Magistrates' Court to the High Court (Administration).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; justices held correct that the Bocker hoist was a trailer and aggregate permissible maximum weight exceeded 3.5 tonnes.
enrichment.ratio: For section 97 Transport Act 1968 read with Regulation 3820/85 Article 4, a non-goods-carrying piece of engineering plant towed behind a motor vehicle is a 'trailer' whose notional maximum gross weight under the 1976 Regulations must be aggregated with the motor vehicle's plated weight to determine whether tachograph equipment is required.
legal_issues: Whether a Bocker H16 hoist is a 'trailer' within EEC Regulation 3820/85 Article 1(2)(c)
How to calculate 'permissible maximum weight' including engineering plant under section 108 Road Traffic Act 1988 and the 1976 Regulations
Whether only goods-carrying trailers count toward the Article 4 3.5-tonne exemption

enrichment.short_title: Planning permission quashed where inspector gave no intelligible reasons on residential amenity space compliance
key_facts: Wycombe District Council refused planning permission for the White Blackbird apartment block in High Wycombe on dominance and amenity-space grounds.
An Inspector granted permission on appeal, treating amenity space as a minor concern under 'Other Matters'.
The Council's adopted and emerging local plans required usable outdoor amenity space with qualitative and minimum size guidelines.
The developer argued purchasers could choose units with less private space and PPG3 supported wider housing choice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash the Secretary of State's planning appeal decision, defended by the developer.
enrichment.outcome: Inspector's decision quashed for inadequate reasons and misdirection on PPG3; costs ordered against Secretary of State to 23 May and against developer thereafter.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector must clearly decide and explain whether a proposed development accords with the development plan when amenity space is a principal controversial issue; invoking PPG3's emphasis on choice cannot displace the section 54A requirement to determine plan compliance and, if departing from plan policies, to conduct an explicit balancing exercise with intelligible reasons.
legal_issues: Adequacy of reasons under Save Britain's Heritage principles
Whether the inspector determined compliance with adopted and emerging local plan amenity-space policies
Proper relationship between PPG3 flexibility and local plan policies already reflecting PPG3
Section 54A development plan compliance and departures

enrichment.short_title: Section 31(7B) capitalisation cannot reopen settled capital claims; Cornick (No 3) wider redistribution rejected
key_facts: Following 1997 consent order the wife received £36,000 per annum periodical payments for life and use of an Italian holiday home via daughters' ownership.
The husband applied under section 31(7B) to capitalise maintenance; the wife sought increase to £60,000 and capitalisation.
Hedley J assessed needs at £47,000 per annum, capitalised at £635,000, then uplifted to £740,000 including mortgage relief and 'sharing'.
The husband's income had fallen from about £270,000 to £130,000 while capital exceeded £1.25m.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) against Hedley J's variation and capitalisation order; permission granted on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; lump sum on capitalisation reduced from £740,000 to £655,000; court held section 31(7B) does not permit general redistribution of capital beyond fair substitution for the discharged maintenance order.
enrichment.ratio: On dismissal of periodical payments under section 31(7B) Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 the court's task is substitution—fairly capitalising the varied maintenance order and completing the clean break—not reopening capital claims compromised in the original order; Charles J's broader construction in Cornick (No 3) was obiter and wrong, and mortgage servicing or debt relief for post-order losses cannot be revisited through section 31(7B).
legal_issues: Scope of discretion under section 31(7A) and (7B) on capitalisation applications
Whether White v White sharing principles apply at the capitalisation stage
Correct treatment of mortgage costs, debt relief, holiday-home undertaking and backdating
Priority of pension-sharing orders under section 31(7B)(ba) where available

enrichment.short_title: Dishonest director must account for all pipeline-loan profits; equitable compensation claim fails for lack of causation
key_facts: Mr Koshy, managing director of Zambian joint venture company GVDC, arranged pipeline loan transactions between GVDC and his company Lasco in 1987-88 without disclosing his personal profit.
GVDC's cotton and wheat farm project at Sinazongwe collapsed; litigation began in 1996 seeking an account of profits and equitable compensation.
Rimer J ordered an account but limited its scope and refused compensation finding no loss caused by non-disclosure.
Both Koshy and GVDC appealed on limitation, scope of account, and compensation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) from Rimer J's judgment after a two-month trial in the GVDC action begun November 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Koshy's appeal dismissed; GVDC's appeal allowed in part so the account covers all profits from the pipeline loan (general account ordered); compensation appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: A director who deliberately and dishonestly conceals his interest in company transactions must account for all unauthorised profits and cannot rely on articles or general law excusing non-disclosure; a claim for an account of profits based on fraudulent breach of trust is not time-barred under section 21(1)(a) Limitation Act 1980, but equitable compensation requires proof that disclosure would have changed GVDC's conduct—and absent such causation the remedy is an account of profits, not loss compensation.
legal_issues: Scope of account of profits for dishonest breach of fiduciary duty
Whether articles or shareholder acquiescence excused failure to disclose self-dealing
Application of section 21 Limitation Act 1980 to account of profits claims
Causation and availability of equitable compensation for non-disclosure
Constructive trust treatment of sums paid to Lasco

enrichment.short_title: Habeas corpus refused in German manslaughter extradition where identity established and delay not oppressive
key_facts: Mark Richard Osawe challenged committal pending extradition to Germany for a 1993 Kassel manslaughter allegedly committed by Oghionmwam Festus Ogieva-Okumbor.
German photographs from 1993 and fingerprint comparison linked the applicant to the wanted person; he accepted the photographs depicted him.
He had lived in the UK since 1995 with a wife, child and outstanding asylum claim.
Authority to proceed named both Ogieva-Okumbor and Osawe; Secretary of State authorised return in April 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum following Bow Street committal under Part III Extradition Act 1989 in a European Convention accusation case.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; committal upheld on identity and section 11 delay grounds; costs application from central funds adjourned with liberty to apply.
enrichment.ratio: In a Convention accusation extradition case the committal court need not go behind a valid authority to proceed where the offence is an extradition crime; identity is sufficiently established by accepted photographs and fingerprints; delay since 1993 does not make return unjust or oppressive under section 11(3)(b) where the applicant appears to have used an alias, German authorities pursued the case, and a fair trial in Germany is assured.
legal_issues: Whether the applicant is the person named in the extradition request and authority to proceed
Construction of section 7(2) particulars requirements where names differ
Whether ten-year delay made return unjust or oppressive under section 11(3)(b)
Interaction of family life and pending asylum claim with extradition delay
